pharm: Antilithic (kidney stone prophylaxis) / potassium and magnesium salt
quick: Trial regimen ~42 mEq potassium / 21 mEq magnesium / 63 mEq citrate per day, divided
Take with meals and plenty of fluids
No reproduction studies; use only if clearly needed
No specific adjustment; citrate metabolized to bicarbonate
Serum potassium, magnesium, renal function; urinary citrate/pH; ECG
summary: Potassium magnesium citrate is an oral urinary alkalinizer and electrolyte replenisher used to prevent recurrent calcium oxalate (and uric acid) kidney stones. Metabolism of citrate produces an alkaline load that raises urinary pH and citrate, which complexes calcium and inhibits stone crystallization; magnesium also inhibits stone formation, and potassium plus magnesium correct depletion. In a randomized trial it markedly reduced recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis. The main hazard is hyperkalemia (and hypermagnesemia), so it is contraindicated in significant renal insufficiency and requires electrolyte monitoring. (Note: the FDA-labeled single citrate product is potassium citrate, Urocit-K; the combination regimen comes from clinical trials.)
indications: Prevention of recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis (kidney stones)
Hypocitraturic calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis (raises urinary citrate and pH)
Uric acid lithiasis with or without calcium stones
Renal tubular acidosis with calcium stones (per the citrate-salt class)

dosage.d: Potassium magnesium citrate providing ~42 mEq potassium, 21 mEq magnesium and 63 mEq citrate per day, in divided doses
Start 60 mEq citrate/day (e.g., 30 mEq twice daily or 20 mEq three times daily)
Start 30 mEq citrate/day (e.g., 15 mEq twice daily or 10 mEq three times daily)

admin: Take orally with meals or within 30 minutes after meals
Maintain high fluid intake (aim for at least about 2 liters of urine daily)
Swallow extended-release tablets whole - do not crush or chew
Avoid concurrent potassium supplements or salt substitutes unless directed
moa: Metabolism of absorbed citrate produces an alkaline (bicarbonate) load that increases urinary pH and raises urinary citrate by augmenting citrate excretion. Urinary citrate complexes with calcium, lowering calcium-salt saturation and inhibiting nucleation and crystallization of calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate. Magnesium independently complexes oxalate and inhibits stone formation, while potassium and magnesium correct any depletion. The higher urine pH also increases uric acid solubility.

absolute: Hyperkalemia or conditions predisposing to it (chronic renal failure, uncontrolled diabetes, acute dehydration, untreated Addison's disease, extensive tissue breakdown)
Significant renal insufficiency (GFR <0.7 mL/kg/min) - risk of soft-tissue calcification and hyperkalemia
relative: Delayed gastric emptying, esophageal compression or GI obstruction (extended-release forms)
Active urinary tract infection (with struvite stones)
monitor: Concurrent potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs or NSAIDs

preg: Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
lact: Use during breastfeeding only if clearly needed.
renal: Contraindicated in significant renal insufficiency (GFR <0.7 mL/kg/min) and severe renal impairment because of the risk of hyperkalemia, hypermagnesemia and soft-tissue calcification. Monitor serum creatinine.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is described; citrate is metabolized to bicarbonate. Use clinical judgment.

major: Potassium-sparing diuretics (triamterene, spironolactone, amiloride) - avoid; risk of severe hyperkalemia
ACE inhibitors and ARBs - potassium retention; monitor potassium closely
moderate: Digoxin - electrolyte shifts (K/Mg) affect glycoside toxicity; monitor
Aluminum-containing antacids - citrate increases aluminum absorption (avoid in renal impairment)
minor: Anticholinergics - may increase GI irritation from extended-release forms
interactions.food: Take with meals and plenty of fluids to reduce GI upset and maintain dilute urine.
interactions.diagnostics: May raise serum potassium and bicarbonate, and increase urinary citrate and pH.

serious: Hyperkalemia - potentially fatal and may be asymptomatic, with risk of cardiac arrhythmia/arrest
GI mucosal lesions/bleeding with extended-release formulations

monitoring: Serum electrolytes (sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate/CO2) and serum magnesium
Serum creatinine / renal function and CBC periodically (e.g., every ~4 months; more often in cardiac, renal or acidotic patients)
24-hour urinary citrate and pH for therapeutic efficacy
counsel: Take with meals and plenty of fluids; do not crush or chew extended-release tablets
Report severe vomiting, abdominal pain or any GI bleeding (black stools)
Report muscle weakness, palpitations or irregular heartbeat (possible high potassium)
Avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes and potassium-sparing diuretics unless your doctor directs
Keep fluid intake high to keep your urine dilute and help prevent stones
pk: Urinary citrate and pH rise after absorption
Citrate absorbed and metabolized to bicarbonate
Sustained effect with divided daily dosing
Store in a tight container at room temperature
pearls: Citrate raises urinary citrate and pH, which inhibits calcium stone formation - benefit shown even without baseline hypocitraturia
Contraindicated in significant renal insufficiency due to hyperkalemia and hypermagnesemia risk
Avoid combining with potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs or NSAIDs without monitoring potassium
FDA-labeled single citrate product is potassium citrate (Urocit-K); the K/Mg citrate combination regimen derives from clinical trials
missed: Take the missed dose when remembered with food and fluids. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule. Do not double the dose.
overdose: Overdose causes hyperkalemia (and hypermagnesemia). Discontinue and eliminate potassium sources; monitor the ECG for arrhythmia. Treatment of hyperkalemia includes IV calcium gluconate for membrane stabilization, insulin with dextrose, sodium bicarbonate for acidosis, and hemodialysis if needed. Severe hypermagnesemia is managed with IV calcium and dialysis in renal failure.
